specAnchors.text: identify common materials which are electrical conductors or insulators, including metals and plastics (physics only)

primer.text: Whether charge can move through a material decides everything about how it behaves in a circuit. Metals brim with delocalised electrons and conduct freely; plastics, rubber, glass and wood have no free charges and block the flow. This note sorts the everyday materials and explains the atomic picture behind the split.

modules.title: Conductors & delocalised electrons
modules.opening: Metals conduct because their outermost electrons are not attached to any single atom: they form a mobile crowd around the positive ions. Since current is a flow of electrons, the freer that crowd moves, the better the metal conducts. Silver, copper, aluminium and steel are the everyday examples.
keyPoints: A conductor lets charge, usually electrons, flow through it easily.
Typical conductors are metals: silver, copper, aluminium and steel.
Metal lattices hold positive ions surrounded by delocalised outer electrons.
Those free electrons make metals good conductors, since current is a flow of electrons.
Plastics and rubbers are insulators — no free charges — so they sheath cables safely.

low.restatement: Metals conduct because their electrons are free to move; the metal ions themselves stay put.
low.analogy: A crowd in a stadium: the seats (ions) never move, but the spectators (electrons) can shuffle along the rows.
low.examPointer: Name four conducting metals if asked to identify common conductors.

medium.restatement: Conductivity is a statement about charge carriers: the more mobile the delocalised electrons, the larger the current a given push produces.
medium.analogy: A motorway versus lanes of parked cars — the freer the traffic, the bigger the flow for the same speed limit.
medium.examPointer: Tie the atomic picture to the definition: delocalised electrons are why the current flows.

modules.title: Insulators & static build-up
modules.opening: An insulator holds its charges hostage: with nothing free to move, any charge deposited on its surface stays where it landed. Rubber, plastic, glass and wood all behave this way. That immobility sounds like a weakness, but it is exactly what lets insulators hold a static charge — and what makes them safe sheaths.
keyPoints: An insulator has no free charges, so charge cannot travel through it easily.
Rubber, plastic, glass and wood are everyday insulators.
Some non-metals conduct a little in the form of static electricity.
Charge can gather on insulator surfaces and pass across when two of them touch.

low.restatement: Insulators have no free charges, so charge stays where it is put on their surfaces.
low.analogy: A parking lot with no exits: cars (charge) can enter but cannot drive through.
low.examPointer: Insulators are not 'nothing happens' materials — they hold static charge, which matters later in this topic.

medium.restatement: The absence of mobile carriers explains both safety uses (sheathing) and static phenomena (charge accumulating on surfaces).
medium.analogy: A sponge that cannot drip: whatever water lands on it, stays on it, until something touches it.
medium.examPointer: Quote the everyday insulators: rubber, plastic, glass, wood.

glossary.definition: A material that lets charge flow through it easily; metals are the everyday examples.
A material with no free charges, so charge cannot travel through it easily.
Metal outer electrons free to move through the lattice — the carriers of the current.
Charge held on an insulator's surface, able to pass across only on contact.
